title: Pastebin
seoTitle: Design a Text Sharing Service Like Pastebin
description: Design Pastebin — storing text snippets, generating short shareable links, expiring pastes, and serving reads cheaply from blob storage and a CDN.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Pastebin?
blocks.text: Pastebin lets anyone paste a block of text — code, logs, notes — and get back a short link they can share. Anyone with the link can read it until it expires.

items: Users should be able to create a paste (up to 10MB of text) and receive a unique short URL.
Users should be able to read a paste by visiting its URL.
Users should be able to set an optional expiration time.
User accounts, editing and syntax highlighting.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Reads should be fast (< 200ms) and highly available.
Paste URLs must be unique and hard to guess.
Storage must be durable — a paste never disappears before it expires.
Scale to 10M new pastes per day and a 10:1 read-to-write ratio.
**Paste**: an ID, the content (or a pointer to it), size, created and expiry times.

blocks.text: 1) Users should be able to create a paste

The **Paste Service** generates an ID, writes the content to **blob storage** (S3) keyed by that ID, and stores small metadata (ID, size, expiry, S3 key) in a database. Content can be up to 10MB, so it doesn't belong in a database row.
2) Users should be able to read a paste

Reads look up the metadata (to check expiry) and return the content. Because pastes never change after creation, they are perfect for caching: serve them through a **CDN** with a TTL that never exceeds the paste's remaining lifetime.
Store `expiresAt` and check it on every read (return `404`/`410` once passed). Use S3 lifecycle rules or a periodic cleanup job to delete expired content so storage doesn't grow forever.
1) How do we generate unique, unguessable IDs?

approach.text: Use the database's sequence and encode it in base62.

challenges.text: IDs are sequential, so anyone can enumerate every paste — a real problem when people paste secrets by accident.

approach.text: Generate 8 random base62 characters (62^8 ≈ 218 trillion possibilities) and insert with a uniqueness constraint; retry on the rare collision.

challenges.text: Very low collision probability at this scale; the retry path is simple. A cryptographically secure RNG makes IDs hard to guess.

approach.text: A background **Key Generation Service** fills a table with unused random IDs. Writers claim a batch of keys and use them locally, so the write path never waits on collision checks.

challenges.text: More moving parts; keys claimed by a crashed server are simply lost, which is harmless.

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep reads fast and cheap?

Pastes are immutable, so cache aggressively. The CDN serves popular pastes from the edge; behind it, an in-memory cache holds hot metadata. Small pastes (under a few KB) can be inlined in the metadata row to avoid a second fetch from S3, while large ones stream straight from blob storage.
Compress content before storing it. Plain text compresses 5-10×, which cuts storage and transfer costs dramatically.

quiz.question: Why store paste content in blob storage instead of the database?
options: Pastes can be up to 10MB, which bloats rows and is cheaper in object storage
quiz.explanation: Large immutable blobs belong in object storage; the database keeps small metadata.

quiz.question: What is the risk of sequential paste IDs?
quiz.explanation: Random IDs prevent people from iterating through other users' pastes.

quiz.question: Why are pastes ideal for CDN caching?
quiz.explanation: Immutable content can be cached safely; just cap the TTL at the remaining lifetime.

quiz.question: How should expired pastes be handled?
options: Check expiresAt on read and clean up storage periodically
quiz.explanation: Read-time checks enforce expiry immediately; lifecycle jobs reclaim storage.
